trails.title: The camera head
trails.subtitle: a frozen DINOv2 embedding beside a measured capture signature, read by a booster
trails.say: How the camera head learns its take on a camera image: a frozen DINOv2 embedding of what the image depicts and the measured capture signature in one row, a features-only store of such rows, a booster grown from scratch or by warm start, and its place in the stack as the combiner's anchor.

steps.title: Why a camera head, and why these two inputs
steps.primer: The camera head is one member of the stack: the detector's take on whether a camera made the image. It reads two kinds of evidence in one row: what the image depicts, from a frozen DINOv2 embedding, and how it was captured, from the capture signature. Joining different evidence as columns of one model is called feature-level fusion. Until 2026-10-21 the row also held a warp score and three sharpness values, and the research measured that they added almost nothing beside the other two.

entries.note: The camera head's row: DINOv2's 384-value embedding, then the nine capture values, 393 columns in the head's own order. A model trained on one column order and run on another would read the capture peak where it expects an embedding value.

deeper.text: Scratch refits scored on 22,703 held-out store rows on 2026-10-19: without the warp score the head lost 0.0012 AUC, without sharpness it gained 0.0002, both at the noise floor of a re-seed; without DINOv2 or without capture it lost more than 0.02.

steps.title: DINOv2: a frozen, self-supervised backbone
steps.primer: DINOv2 is a vision transformer trained without labels to describe images, so that similar images land near each other in its embedding space. VeilGarde reads its small model as a frozen feature extractor: the CLS token, a 384-value summary of the whole image, is read out, and the network is never fine-tuned. Its embedding places a portrait near other portraits and a watercolour near other watercolours, an axis a camera measurement cannot see. Alone it is no detector; beside the physical evidence it is.

entries.note: Runs DINOv2-small's twelve transformer blocks over the 16×16 patches of a 224-pixel input and returns the CLS token, the 384-value embedding of the whole image. The same pass also yields the patch tokens the semantic-tile head reads.

deeper.text: The research's probe found every semantic and physical feature tied to the data it was trained on, with no feature that holds across unseen generators; the fusion works because each axis covers another's blind spot. Quoted from the research.

entries.anchor: let resized = TorchBicubic.resize(planes, planes: dim, input: side, output: target)
entries.note: DINOv2 is imported, not trained here: the import renames Hugging Face's tensors and resizes the 37×37 position grid to 16×16 for a 224-pixel input. That resize must be PyTorch's bicubic, bit for bit, or the file would differ from the shipped export.

deeper.text: The imported small file is byte-identical to the shipped export, and the F16 variant's tensors equal the reference export's.
deeper.cite: test:small is byte-identical to the shipped export; xsmall's tensors are Garde's

entries.note: The DINOv2 weights are a frozen role with CLIP's: the flywheel may never promote over them. Every head and the fusion were trained on this embedding, and only frozen weights keep it the one they read.

steps.title: One backbone, several readings
steps.primer: Preprocessing is part of a model. A network that learned from images resized one way gives a different embedding of the same image resized another way, so each model on top must be fed the way it was trained. VeilGarde reads DINOv2 three ways: the camera head reads the CLS of a plain crop, every specialist head reads the CLS after a forced 360 by 640 resize, and the semantic-tile head reads the patch tokens. The store keeps both CLS embeddings as separate columns.

entries.note: The camera head's embedding: the CLS after the plain preprocessing, the short edge to 256 and a centre crop of 224. The camera head reads this path and every linear head the force-resized one, two embeddings of one image that the store keeps apart.

entries.anchor: ctx.draw(cg, in: CGRect(x: -cropX, y: -cropY, width: sw, height: sh))
entries.note: Scales the short edge to 256, crops the centre 224 square, and normalizes by ImageNet's mean and standard deviation, as Hugging Face's processor does. The heads' path force-resizes first, so a phone screenshot's resolution cannot leak into their embedding.

steps.title: The capture signature: a measured input
steps.primer: The capture signature is measured, not learned. A camera's sensor and demosaicing leave a periodic trace at the highest frequencies of its native pixels; a generator's output and an image that was resized lose it. Its nine values enter the camera row as they are, and the capture member reports it in the stack, where a present trace silences every generated-side member. It is read at native resolution, so a crop keeps it and a resize removes it.

entries.note: One measurement in two forms: the nine values the camera head reads, and the signature the capture member reports: the spectral peak, whether the image is large enough to measure, its native short side, and whether the peak is present.

A valid signature counts as present at a peak of 30 or more, on a native short side of at least 512 pixels. Below that size the peak is not reliable, and the signature is marked invalid instead of absent.
The four fields the capture member reports in every result's stack, and the store's rows carry as nine values with the measurements behind them.

steps.title: The data: a store of features, weighted
steps.primer: The camera head trains on stored features, not images. Each row holds what the head reads, already measured, so a retrain reads the store and never an image. Rows are weighted, so the kinds of image the head must learn hardest count more. A share of the newest generators' rows is held out, so the recall reported on them is on rows the head never trained on.

entries.anchor: for column in CameraRow.columns { x.append(contentsOf: selection.vector(column, row: i)) }
entries.note: Takes every store row that is not golden, not NSFW and carries the plain embedding, ordered by id, and stacks its DINOv2 and capture columns. The store keeps three columns since 2026-10-21.

deeper.text: On 2026-10-21 that was 113,195 rows, with 1,569 of 5,263 new-generator rows held out and 11,212 rows set aside for the evaluation twin.

entries.note: The row weights and two holdouts: new-generator rows, the flux family at 0.7, preview rows and emphasized ids each carry a weight; 30% of the new-generator rows stay out of training, and a twin is fitted without a further 10% of all rows to report a held-out AUC.

steps.title: The algorithm: trees, from scratch or by warm start
steps.primer: The camera head is a gradient-boosted ensemble of shallow decision trees over 393 columns: each tree is fitted to the errors the trees before it leave, at a small learning rate. A booster retrained from scratch does not reproduce the old one's decision boundary, so it can lose cases the old one got right. A warm start keeps every existing tree and adds a few, so the boundary moves a little at a time. The shipped head was trained from scratch on 2026-10-21, because the 397-column head before it could not be continued on 393 columns.

entries.anchor: public static let flywheel = CameraMode.warmStart(add: 80, eta: 0.03)
entries.note: Two ways to train: a warm start that adds 80 trees at a learning rate of 0.03, the flywheel's way to move the camera head, or 500 trees from scratch at 0.04, the way the shipped head was trained.

deeper.text: Under the warp era a warm start of 80 trees raised held-out recall from 0.9955 to 0.9975 and still failed the battery, flipping IMG_0291 from 0.757 to 0.184; a 20-tree start passed. Measured on the 397-column head on 2026-10-19.

entries.anchor: guard let parent else { throw VeilGardeFailure.missing("a warm start needs the parent camera head") }
entries.note: Fits the evaluation twin and scores it on rows it never saw, then trains on every row not held out. A warm start hands the parent to the booster, which keeps its trees byte for byte, and a parent of another width is refused.

deeper.text: The shipped head's twin, 2026-10-21: AUC 0.9817, real false-positive rate 0.052 and generated recall 0.918 at 0.5 on 11,212 held-out rows; recall on the held-out new generators 0.978.

steps.title: What it adds to the result
steps.primer: The camera head's probability is its own row of the stack, called at 0.5. The combiner revision anchors on it unless the screenshot gate fired, and on an image with no capture signature weighs the specialist members against it: the anchor enters with the largest weight, under a cap no member can outweigh.

entries.anchor: return MemberOutput(name: name, p: p, verdict: s.config.decision.label(p), fields: [Field("p_neutral", .number(pNeutral))])
entries.note: Calls the head's probability at 0.5 with a band of 0.04 either side, its own verdict in the stack. The screenshot member reports beside it, and the combiner, not the camera member, decides which one anchors.
The bounded logit every input enters the combiner through. The anchor's cap is twice an evidence member's and its weight the largest, so a saturated member cannot overturn a confident anchor.

trails.title: The specialist heads
trails.subtitle: linear probes on DINOv2's frozen embedding, stacked under a non-negative combiner
trails.say: How the specialist heads learn the sectors the camera head misses: each a standardized logistic probe trained on DINOv2's frozen embedding from a features-only store, split by source, admitted only if it leaves real photographs alone, a member of the stack with its own score, pooled around the camera head by a small non-negative combiner, and grown every week by the flywheel.

steps.title: Why specialists, and why a stack
steps.primer: The camera head is strong where it was trained and weaker in a few sectors: AI art against human art, generative blur against a camera's, photoreal people against real portraits. A specialist is a small model that knows one of those questions well. Each is its own member of the stack with its own score, and the combiner revision weighs their evidence against the anchor under caps no member can exceed.

entries.note: Names every linear head by its role: the screenshot member's content head, the three category heads the combiner pools, the preview head the preview tail reads, and the semantic-tile head. The three category heads enter the combiner in a fixed order, art, blur, human.

entries.anchor: guard let head = HeadRegistry.shared.head(kind, in: s.config.bundle) else { return nil }
entries.note: Scores one head on the image and records it as its own row of the stack. A head that is not in the bundle leaves no row, so a head is added by a file and one line in the pipeline, not by new code.

deeper.text: The research tried a monolithic combiner that blended every signal, and real false positives rose from 8% to between 50% and 92%; the stack holds them at 0%. Quoted from the research.

steps.title: The embedding they read
steps.primer: Every head reads the same frozen DINOv2 network as the fusion head, through another door: the image is first forced to 360 by 640 pixels. A portrait and a landscape are then read at the same shape, and a source's resolution cannot leak into the embedding. Nothing here fine-tunes DINOv2. Each head is a small linear model trained on top of the frozen embedding, which is called a linear probe.

entries.note: The heads' embedding: the CLS token after the image is force-resized to 360 by 640. Every head was trained on this embedding, and the store keeps it as its own column, dino_norm, apart from the camera head's.

entries.anchor: let dinoNorm = columns.contains(.dinoNorm) ? try SemanticLens.normalizedEmbedding(cg, variant: variant) : nan384
entries.note: Measures one image into the store's three columns with the detector's own calls, in the detector's order, so a stored row is what inference would compute for that image. The image is read, measured and dropped.

deeper.text: The store holds 138,267 rows in 60 shards, migrated to the v1 shard format on 2026-10-21; the heads, the camera head and the combiner all train on such rows.

steps.title: The algorithm: a standardized logistic probe
steps.primer: Each head is logistic regression: a weighted sum of the 384 embedding values plus an intercept, through a sigmoid. Each value is standardized first, its mean subtracted and divided by its spread, so no dimension dominates by its scale. L2 regularization at C 0.5 keeps the weights small, and class weights balance generated against real. A new head is a new file of numbers, not new code.

entries.note: Computes P(AI) as the sigmoid of the coefficients times the standardized embedding plus the intercept, in Float and in index order, as the reference does. Every specialist is this one primitive with its own numbers.
Each column's mean and population standard deviation over the training rows. A constant column scales by 1 and passes through centred, as sklearn's scaler does.

Solves sklearn's L2-regularized logistic objective exactly by Newton's method, with balanced class weights when asked. The problem is strictly convex, so the exact optimum is the target sklearn's own solver approaches, and there was no reason to port that solver.

deeper.text: The head recipes reach sklearn's optimum within 1e-5.

steps.title: The data, and a split by source
steps.primer: Each head learns its own positives against its own negatives, chosen from the store: AI art against museum and human art, for one. Its test rows come from sources it never trained on. A source-disjoint split tests whether a head learned the generator rather than the look of one website, which a random split cannot.

entries.anchor: let fit = LogisticNewton.fit(x: scaler.transform(x, d: d, rows: train), y: train.map(label), d: d, C: settings.C, classWeight: settings.classWeight)
entries.note: Takes the usable store rows, splits them by source, fits the scaler and the regression at C 0.5 with balanced classes, and measures the head on the held-out sources and on golden reals. A head needs at least 50 training rows and 10 test rows.

deeper.text: Retrained from the seed store, test AUC against the shipped head on the same rows: art 0.9774 against 0.9439 on the id split, blur 0.9629 against 0.9177, cgi 0.9847 against 0.9668, and human 0.6713 against 0.6955 on the source-disjoint split.

entries.note: Holds out a quarter of the sources, shuffled as the research's script shuffled them. When that leaves a class out of the test rows, where AUC is undefined, it falls back to an id split and records that it did.

entries.anchor: case .semtile: return "the semantic-tile head trains on DINOv2 patch tokens, which the store does not keep"
entries.note: Refuses the screenshot and semantic-tile heads before any work, with the reason: the store holds no screenshot rows and keeps no patch tokens. Training them on proxies was rejected.

steps.title: Admission: a rule at the operating point
steps.primer: A good AUC does not make a head safe to ship. What matters is what it does at the threshold where it fires, and a head that blocks real photographs is worse than no head. So a head is admitted only if, at 0.8, it flags at most one in ten of a set of golden real images, whatever its AUC.

entries.anchor: return Admission(anchors: anchors, block: block, admitted: block <= admissionCeiling)
entries.note: Scores a candidate head on the store's golden reals outside Bluesky and admits it only if it blocks at most 10% of them at 0.8. A head that blocks real images is worse than no head.

deeper.text: Retrained from the seed store, every atlas head was admitted: art blocked 1.6% against the shipped head's 4.7%, blur 6.2% against 9.4%, human and cgi none.

entries.note: Every promote check runs before live is touched: a category head must pass admission, the camera head must keep live's trees byte for byte, a combiner's weights must all be at least zero and its members held by live. A refusal leaves live as it was.

steps.title: The combiner: pooling with signs and caps
steps.primer: The combiner is a second, tiny model on top: logistic regression over the anchor and the evidence members, which is called stacking. Its weights are held at zero or above, so a member that reads real can never push toward generated. Generated evidence adds; real evidence subtracts only while the anchor is unsure, under 0.75. When every evidence member reads real, a rescue pulls toward real by the weakest of their real readings.

entries.anchor: if a < anchor.gateCeiling { z -= rescue.w * max(0, -maxLogit) }
entries.note: Pools the capped anchor logit and each evidence member's positive logit times its weight, then, while the anchor is under the gate, subtracts the rescue. A saturated member can never overturn a confident anchor.

entries.anchor: for row in features { var r = row; r[4] = 0; flat.append(contentsOf: r) }
entries.note: Fits the weights as a logistic regression held at zero or above, real rows counted three times, with the rescue column zeroed because the corpus cannot teach it.

deeper.text: Refit on 97,166 capture-absent store rows, the pooled test AUC is 0.9901 against the camera head's 0.9896 and the real false-positive rate falls from 3.1% to 1.2%. It is a new fit, not a reproduction of the shipped weights, which were fitted on another cache.

entries.anchor: if real == settings.probes.count && top <= settings.maxProbe && chosen == 0 { chosen = candidate }
entries.note: Chooses the rescue weight by a sweep that must keep every protect-real probe real and none above 0.42, taking the first of 0.5, 0.8, 1.0 and 1.3 that does, else the fallback. On the 2026-10-21 refit none did, so the combiner ships with the fallback, 1.0.

steps.title: How the heads grow: the flywheel
steps.primer: A detector trained once falls behind as generators change. The flywheel finds where the camera head is wrong, fetches images of that kind, keeps only their features, and every week trains candidate heads and a warm-started camera head on top of the live bundle. A candidate reaches live only through promote, behind admission and a battery of images the detector must never get wrong. The backbones never move.

entries.note: The weekly recipe: the three category heads from the whole store, and the camera head warm-started by 80 trees at 0.03, trained on top of live into a candidate bundle. Nothing here writes live.

The flywheel's north-star number: how often the camera head alone reaches the same call as the pooled verdict. The flywheel's job is to make the camera head trustworthy on more images, so the agreement should climb.

deeper.text: The first weekly candidate raised it from 0.9857 to 0.9894 on the store. The live models were trained on store rows, so these are not held-out numbers.

entries.anchor: // Back up, then write beside and rename in.
entries.note: Promote is the only writer of live: it snapshots live, writes the slot, re-pins the manifest and runs the battery the slot needs, and restores the snapshot on a failure.

deeper.text: On its first day it refused the weekly camera head: the 80 new trees flipped IMG_0291 from 0.757 to 0.184, and live was restored.

trails.title: One verdict
trails.subtitle: a stack of independent members, three revisions, one result
trails.say: How several models give one answer: the signals computed once, every member of the stack its own score, the combiner anchored on one of them, two more revisions on decisive evidence, one result that records it all, and fixed rules that ask whether each part earns its place.

steps.title: One image, one number
steps.primer: A detector built from several models still has to give one answer. VeilGarde computes the shared signals once, runs every member of its stack, then three revisions in a fixed order. The first sets the verdict around one anchor; the others move it only on evidence they are built to trust, so the final number keeps the anchor's meaning: P(AI), called at 0.5.

entries.note: Computes the signals once, collects every member's output in the declared order, then runs the revisions in theirs, each reading the stack and recording what it did.
The one result: the verdict and its operating point, the image's size, every member's output and every revision's record.

steps.title: The stack: every member speaks
steps.primer: No member routes the image to another. The screenshot gate is a signal: the screenshot member reports it beside its head's score, and the combiner uses it to choose its anchor, never image size, because size says little about where an image came from. Every other member reads the same signals and says what it sees.

entries.note: Asks every member in turn; each answers from the shared signals alone, and none reads another's answer.
Reports the gate's three tells and whether they fire together, beside the screenshot head's own score.

steps.title: The combiner revision
steps.primer: Stacking means each member adds evidence around an anchor instead of being blended with it. The combiner anchors on the camera member, or the screenshot member when the gate fired. A valid, present capture signature is the strongest sign of a camera, so it leaves the anchor standing and silences the generated-side members. Without one, a small non-negative combiner pools the anchor with the art, blur and human members, and a rescue term pulls an image toward real when every one of them reads real.

entries.note: Reads the anchor, then the capture member: a present signature leaves the anchor standing, otherwise the evidence members are pooled around it.

entries.anchor: if l > 0 { return (k < evidence.count ? evidence[k].w : 0) * l }
entries.note: An evidence member's influence, kept in the combiner's record: its generated push, or the shared rescue while every member reads real under the gate.

deeper.text: The research tried a monolithic combiner that blended every signal, and real false positives rose from 8% to between 50% and 92%; the stack holds them at 0%. Quoted from the research.

steps.title: Revisions on decisive evidence
steps.primer: Two more revisions can overturn the combiner, each only on evidence that is decisive for its own case. A dark frame around the content can hide it, so the frame seam runs the pipeline again on the interior. A small preview has no valid capture signature, so the preview tail reads the camera member's p_neutral, its score with that shortcut neutralized.

entries.note: Takes the interior's verdict only when it reads at least 0.70 and at least 0.20 above the framed one.

deeper.text: In the 2026-10-19 census it ran on 3 of 300 images and decided one, a hard battery anchor.

entries.note: Flips a small image to real only when the preview member and the camera member's p_neutral both read it real.

deeper.text: Zoom escalation, the render taxonomy and the x-domain gate were removed on 2026-10-21; none of them ran by default.

steps.title: One result
steps.primer: The result is one JSON object: the verdict and its operating point, every member's output in the stack, every revision's record, and the bundle's hashes. Schema v1, since 2026-10-21, a clean break from v3. Sorted keys make the same result the same bytes, so a golden file can hold it.

entries.note: What each revision left: the P(AI) and prediction after it, whether it changed them, and its own fields.
Writes exactly schema v1's keys: schema_version, device, image, verdict, stack, revisions, bundle and times_sec.

steps.title: Does each part earn its place?
steps.primer: A part earns its place when the detector without it does worse on images it must get right. VeilGarde measures that three ways: a battery of anchor images it must never miss, a census of labelled images, and a comparison of two detectors' censuses image by image. The rules are fixed before the numbers come in.

entries.note: Runs the battery on a bundle and exits 1 on a failure, so a script cannot miss one.

deeper.text: On 2026-10-21 the detector without the warp failed two hard groups, flux_anchor and user_gen, four images in all.

entries.note: Runs the battery's images and 200 of final_mixed's, records every call with every member's score and every revision's record, and names the bundle it ran.
Joins two censuses image by image and counts the calls that moved to the right label and to the wrong one, against rules fixed in code.

deeper.text: Without the warp score on 2026-10-21, 25 fewer of 200 final_mixed images were called right, 161 to 136, and of 53 moved calls 42 moved to the wrong label.

trails.title: The watermark
trails.subtitle: no model trained: a measured feature, ordinal codes, Hamming similarity and a threshold
trails.say: How the watermark reads a measured residual instead of a learned model: each tile's fragility at native resolution, turned into four ordinal bits that survive recompression, packed so a crop keeps them in place, matched by Hamming similarity over offsets and grid phases, and judged by a kill criterion fixed before the run.

steps.title: The carrier: a measured feature, not an embedded pattern
steps.primer: Most watermarks hide a pattern in the pixels, which an attacker can find and strip. This one adds nothing. Its signature is a feature the warp residual measures, each tile's fragility, read at native resolution so that a crop lands on the same tiles as its source. No model is trained here: the machine-learning questions are about representation, similarity and choosing a threshold.

entries.note: Warps every tile through 16 fixed homographies and back and keeps the high frequencies of what the round trip lost. A camera tile's sensor noise survives it differently from a generator's smooth output.

entries.anchor: let fr = WarpResidual.fragility(low: low, high: high)
entries.note: Measures the fragility rate of every full 32-pixel tile at native resolution, from any tile origin, with the detector's own residual. Nothing is resized, so a crop of the image sees the same tiles, shifted by whole tiles.

steps.title: The code: four ordinal bits a tile
steps.primer: A robust feature survives what an image meets on its way, such as recompression or an exposure shift. Raw fragility values move under such changes, but mostly together, so comparisons between neighbouring tiles survive where the values do not. Each tile becomes four bits, each the answer to one comparison with a neighbour. Coding by order instead of by value is a classic route to invariance under any monotone change.

entries.anchor: if v > g[nr, nc] { bits[r * g.cols + c] |= 1 << k }
entries.note: Gives each tile four bits, whether its fragility exceeds its east, south, south-east and north-east neighbours', and masks a comparison that would leave the grid. Ordinal bits survive any monotone change of the residual's gain, a JPEG or an exposure shift, where quantized levels would not.

deeper.text: Across 198 images each of the four bits split almost evenly, between 0.496 and 0.498, so each bit is close to a fair coin from image to image.

steps.title: Sections: keeping the bits where a crop finds them
steps.primer: A crop keeps a rectangle of the original's tiles, so the signature must keep tiles in place rather than fold them together. Sixteen tiles, four by four, pack into one 64-bit word, with a second word for the masks. No hash folds them: a tile that differs costs one bit of Hamming distance, not a different hash.

entries.note: Packs each 4×4 section's sixteen nibbles into a 64-bit word in row-major order, with its masks beside it. A crop contains whole sections of the image it came from, and the concatenated words are the signature.
The signature's content id is the SHA-256 of its binary bytes, so two signatures of the same pixels are the same id.

steps.title: Matching: similarity, alignment and a score against chance
steps.primer: To match, the crop's codes are slid over the signature's at every whole-tile offset, and the score is the share of measured bits that agree. A crop starts at an arbitrary pixel, so its codes are also read at sixteen sub-tile phases, one of which lies within four pixels of the stored grid. Two unrelated images agree about half the time, so a z-score says how far a score sits above chance for the bits compared.

entries.anchor: out.append((px, py, TileCodeGrid(plane.fragility(originX: px, originY: py))))
entries.note: Reads the image's codes at sixteen grid phases, every 8 pixels in each direction, so one phase sits within 4 pixels of the signed grid. The stored grid is anchored at the image's corner, and a crop at an arbitrary offset cuts tiles that straddle the stored ones.

Slides the crop's codes over the signature's at every whole-tile offset and counts the disagreeing bits among those both sides measured. The score is the share that agree, and a match needs at least 0.75 over at least 256 bits.
The agreement's distance from chance in coin-flip units: the score minus 0.5, over the square root of 0.25 divided by the bits compared. It says how unlikely a score is by luck for that many bits.

deeper.text: The z-score does not replace the floor: every crop sat at least 9.2 above chance, but strangers reached 11.9, because the matcher keeps the best of thousands of placements and the codes are spatially structured.

steps.title: The acceptance: a kill criterion fixed first
steps.primer: v1 was a design under measurement, not a claim. Its kill criterion was written in code before the run: crops must match with their offset in at least 60% of images, the median JPEG score must reach 0.75, and some threshold must reach 80% crop recall with at most 5% false matches. Choosing that threshold is a classifier's operating-point question: recall on crops against false matches on strangers.

entries.anchor: if recall >= 0.80, op == nil || fpr < op!.fpr || (fpr == op!.fpr && t > op!.t) { op = (t, recall, fpr) }
entries.note: Summarizes the run against the criterion: the self-match rate, the crop rate with its offset, the median JPEG score, and the threshold that reaches 80% crop recall with the fewest false matches. Failing any part kills v1.

deeper.text: v1 passed on 198 images: crops matched with their offset in 73.2%, the median JPEG score was 0.958, and at a threshold of 0.73 crop recall was 81.3% with no false matches.

entries.note: Signs each sampled image, then scores a self-match, a random half-area crop, a JPEG re-encode and a cross match against another image's signature, and the crop resized on every fourth image. The resizes were cut to every fourth image before any was measured: they were half of each image's cost and no part of the criterion.

deeper.text: Large camera photographs are v1's weak case: images under 2 megapixels matched 81.6% of the time and images of 2 or more 45.7%, the score falling with the misalignment the 8-pixel phase grid leaves.

entries.note: Signs a fixed set of images again and lists every way a signature departs from the recorded one: the regression test a measured carrier needs, since any change to the residual's arithmetic would change every signature.

deeper.text: After the detection change and again after the residual moved into the watermark on 2026-10-21, all 105 battery images kept their signatures.
